title: 002 — Databricks ai_decide: structured decisions on text, straight from SQL
html:
002 — Databricks ai_decide: structured decisions on text, straight from SQL

The one idea: ai_decide is a Databricks SQL function that answers fixed questions about each row of text (pick a category, give a probability, score on a scale) and returns structured answers with probabilities and confidence. It is built for decisions rather than text generation, so Databricks says it is faster and cheaper than calling a general LLM for the same job.

Added 2026-10-05 · Released 2026-09-30 by Databricks (Beta)

1. What it is

ai_decide is a new Databricks AI Function. You give it a row's content (the state) and a set of questions defined once as JSON. For every row it returns one answer per question, as a VARIANT. You can call it from SQL to tag a whole table, or through a REST API for real-time applications and agents.

Three question types cover most decision work:

Type What it answers What comes back
choice Which of these labels fits? the chosen label, a probability per label, and a confidence
noul Is this statement true? a single probability
score Where on this ordered scale does it sit? a score, the legend, a probability per level, and a confidence

2. Why it matters

Tagging, routing and checking text inside a pipeline is a common job: classify support tickets, flag reviews that mention a defect, decide which model or team a request should go to, grade an answer against criteria. Until now the usual tool was a general LLM call (ai_query or an external API) plus prompt work to force a parseable output. That approach has three problems:

  • Output shape. A generative model can drift from the format you asked for. ai_decide always returns the same typed structure.
  • Calibration. You get probabilities and a confidence, not just a label. That lets a pipeline send uncertain rows to a person, or to a stronger model.
  • Cost and speed. Databricks positions the function as faster and cheaper than LLMs on similar tasks, with answers returned in a fraction of a second.

Because it runs inside Databricks SQL on Unity Catalog tables, the data never leaves the governed platform.

3. How it works

---
title: ai_decide — one call per row, same questions for every row
---
flowchart LR
    T["Table rows<br/>(text or VARIANT)"] --> F["ai_decide(state, questions)"]
    Q["Questions JSON<br/>(constant)"] --> F
    F --> V["VARIANT per row<br/>response.answers"]
    V --> C{"confidence high?"}
    C -- yes --> A["Act automatically"]
    C -- no --> R["Route to review<br/>or a stronger model"]

Signature, from the SQL reference:

ai_decide(state, questions [, options])
  • state (STRING or VARIANT): the content to judge, and any context or examples. It can be plain text, JSON, or the VARIANT output of another AI function. It varies by row.
  • questions (constant STRING): a JSON object. Each key is a question ID, and each value gives the question's type, its instructions, and its criteria. criteria is required except for noul.
  • options (optional constant MAP<STRING, STRING>): currently only version, default '1.0'.

The result is a VARIANT with response.answers (one entry per question), metadata.version, and error_message (null on success).

4. How to use it

Requirements: a workspace admin enables the Beta on the Previews page. You need Databricks SQL (not SQL Classic) on Databricks Runtime 15.4 LTS or above (18.2+ recommended), in a supported region. Usage is billed at Databricks SQL pricing.

The documentation's example asks three questions about one product listing:

SELECT ai_decide(
  '{"name": "TrailShell jacket", "description": "Lightweight waterproof hiking jacket made from recycled polyester. Packs into its own pocket."}',
  '{
    "category": {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": "Which product category best fits this item?",
      "criteria": {
        "outerwear": "Jackets, coats, and other protective outer layers",
        "footwear": "Shoes, boots, and sandals",
        "accessories": "Bags, hats, and other accessories"
      }
    },
    "recycled_materials": {
      "type": "noul",
      "instructions": "Does the listing state that the product uses recycled materials?"
    },
    "hiking_suitability": {
      "type": "score",
      "instructions": "How suitable is this product for hiking in rainy weather?",
      "criteria": [
        "Not suitable for outdoor use in rain",
        "Offers some protection from rain",
        "Designed for hiking with waterproof protection"
      ]
    }
  }',
  map('version', '1.0')
) AS decision;

The response picks outerwear with probability 0.95, gives recycled_materials a probability of 0.98, and scores hiking suitability 1.8 on the 0–2 scale, with probabilities for each level.

In practice, for a table, pass a column as state and keep the questions constant. Then pull fields out of the VARIANT with the : path syntax. The query below is a sketch built on the documented signature and return shape; check it against the docs for your runtime:

SELECT
  ticket_id,
  d:response.answers.category.choice::string      AS category,
  d:response.answers.category.confidence::double  AS confidence
FROM (
  SELECT ticket_id,
         ai_decide(body, '{"category": {"type": "choice",
                                         "instructions": "Which team should handle this ticket?",
                                         "criteria": {"billing": "Payments, invoices, refunds",
                                                      "technical": "Errors, outages, bugs",
                                                      "account": "Login, profile, access"}}}') AS d
  FROM support.tickets
);

Rows with low confidence can then go to a review queue, a pattern that fits well in a medallion pipeline between silver and gold.

5. Trade-offs and limits

  • Beta: the function signature, the question types and the version option may change. Pin map('version', '1.0') so results do not shift silently.
  • Decisions, not prose: it does not write summaries or extract free text. Use ai_query or other AI Functions for that.
  • Platform and region: Databricks SQL only, and not every region (or compliance profile) has it yet.
  • Cost model: it runs on Databricks SQL pricing. Running it over a large table on every refresh still costs compute, so apply it incrementally to new rows.
  • Lock-in: the questions JSON is portable as an idea but not as code. Moving off Databricks means re-implementing it.

6. Where it fits

  • Databricks platform: Databricks SQL, Unity Catalog and AI Functions.
  • Pipeline patterns and practices: incremental processing, so you only score new rows.
  • Orchestration, quality and governance: using confidence thresholds as a data-quality gate.
  • LLM engineering and RAG: when a specialised model beats a general LLM.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What does a noul question return, and how does it differ from a two-label choice?
  2. Why is a calibrated probability more useful to a pipeline than a bare label?
  3. How would you stop ai_decide from re-scoring every row of a large table on each run?
  4. When would you still reach for ai_query instead of ai_decide?
  5. Why pin the version option in a production job?
